papers.title: Inferring modularity in genotype-phenotype maps using patterns of epistasis and pleiotropy
papers.abstract: Methods for inferring the relationship between genotype and phenotype often search for low-dimensional structure, motivated by the hypothesis that genetic loci can be organized into a small number of groups representing biological processes. These methods typically group genetic loci based on which other loci they interact with (epistasis) or based on how their effects covary across environmental conditions (patterns of pleiotropy). Here, we present two complementary methods that combine epistasis and pleiotropy to infer modular structure. The first, Sparse, Low-dimensional, Epistatic Decomposition (SLED), parametrizes the genotype-phenotype map in terms of a small number of modules: loci contribute sparse additive and epistatic effects to modules, and modules contribute sparse additive and epistatic effects to multiple phenotypes. The second method, Graph Tensor Decomposition (GTD), represents the epistatic interactions in each environment as a combination of shared basis graphs, each capturing a pattern of epistasis that recurs across environments. Since GTD does not use additive effects, learned graphs are not restricted to include only loci whose additive effects covary across environments. We validate SLED and GTD on synthetic data, then apply both methods to an experimental dataset consisting of the growth rates of yeast segregants from an F1 cross, measured across 101 environments with a hub-and-spoke structure. We evaluate the biological structure of the inferred modules and show that both models generalize well to held-out environments. Finally, we compare the modules inferred by SLED, GTD, and a previously established method that infers sparse modular structure from a locus-by-environment matrix of additive effects (SSD) and find that all three methods yield highly similar modular architectures. This suggests that the genetic architecture underlying this dataset is consistent across additive effects (SSD), epistatic effects (GTD), and both jointly (SLED). Together, our methods provide a framework for combining two sources of information, epistasis and pleiotropy, to infer interpretable low-dimensional structure in genotype-phenotype maps, expanding on previous work that has traditionally treated each independently.

papers.title: Gene expression in Anolis sagrei suggests conservation of patterning mechanisms drives formation of two high acuity areas
papers.abstract: As humans we enjoy high acuity color vision. A specialized area in our retinas, the fovea, endows us with this ability. Some vertebrates, such as the Anolis sagrei (brown anole), have two such areas. Whether different species use conserved developmental mechanism(s), and whether the same mechanism is used in one organism to pattern both foveae, are herein addressed in the brown anole. We observed that the expression of canonical axis patterning genes is conserved in the anole retina. Retinoic acid and Fgf signaling pathways were found to define two discrete domains corresponding to emerging foveae. Comparative spatial analyses of early gene expression patterns among anole, chick, and human revealed conserved patterns in the anlage of the high acuity areas of each species. Variation in foveal number could arise through spatial redeployment of conserved patterning programs.

papers.title: The mechanism of cysteine sensing by LRRC58
papers.abstract: Cysteine is essential for life but toxic in excess. Cells and tissues are exposed to elevated cysteine from endogenous sources and the environment yet maintain low intracellular concentrations to sustain life. Here we identify a mechanism for sensing cysteine to control its abundance and prevent toxicity and premature death. Using cryo-electron microscopy we determine structures of the CRL5L^RRC58 E3 ligase alone and in complex with the cysteine-catabolizing enzyme CDO1. We show that CDO1 interacts with LRRC58 in the vicinity of a zinc-coordinating cysteine motif, within which Cys296 becomes covalently modified upon cysteine exposure. Covalent modification of Cys296 and zinc ejection from this motif drive large structural rearrangements of LRRC58 relayed through Cys319, which destabilize CDO1 binding and position LRRC58 Lys111 for autoubiquitylation. This reorientation of LRRC58 permits CDO1 accumulation, thereby lowering intracellular cysteine. Mutation of Cys319 abrogates inhibitory rearrangement of LRRC58 upon cysteine modification. This renders the ligase constitutively active and prevents CDO1 stabilization, thereby driving systemic cysteine accumulation and premature death in animals. These findings establish the molecular basis of homeostatic cysteine sensing by LRRC58 and demonstrate its essential role in maintaining cysteine concentrations compatible with healthy life.

papers.title: A mitochondrial orphan protein contributes to sperm development in bivalves
papers.abstract: Lineage-specific genes, or orphan genes, are increasingly recognized as important drivers of evolutionary innovation, yet their functional characterization remains largely restricted to nuclear genomes of model organisms. Whether lineage-specific genes encoded by mitochondrial DNA contribute to phenotypic diversification remains virtually unexplored. Here we investigate MORF, a rapidly evolving ORFan protein encoded by the paternally transmitted mitochondrial genome of bivalves with doubly uniparental inheritance (DUI). Combining immunolocalization, functional neutralization, protein interaction assays and proteomics in the distantly related bivalves Mytilus edulis and Venustaconcha ellipsiformis, we characterize MORF localization, function and molecular associations during male germ cell development. MORF localizes to developing sperm cells and mature sperm mitochondria in both species and is additionally detected in the acrosome of M. edulis. In cultured M. edulis germ cells, antibody-mediated neutralization of MORF increases the frequency of spermatids displaying four rather than the canonical five mitochondria, providing functional evidence that MORF contributes to mitochondrial organization during spermatogenesis. Comparative proteomic analyses identify MORF-associated proteins involved in cytoskeletal organization, protein homeostasis and extracellular matrix organization. The association between MORF and laminin is independently supported by western blotting in both species. Despite extensive sequence divergence, the two MORF proteins display overlapping functional and molecular features. Together, these findings uncover a functional role for a rapidly evolving mitochondrial orphan protein and point to mitochondrial orphan genes as a potentially overlooked source of evolutionary novelty.

papers.title: Squalene as a Candidate Signalling Molecule: Computational Evidence for a Predicted KEAP1 Interaction and Implications for Stress-Induced Altruistic Stem-Cell Niche Protection
papers.abstract: Stem and progenitor cells exposed to cytotoxic stress must preserve both their own viability and the functional integrity of their surrounding niche. Previous investigations from our laboratory have described stress-adapted altruistic stem-cell phenotypes and demonstrated the cytoprotective potential of squalene in normal haematopoietic and mesenchymal progenitor cells through preservation of glutathione homeostasis. More recent studies have associated hypoxia-driven changes in squalene metabolism with intracellular squalene accumulation and protection against lipid peroxidation, while independent experimental evidence has implicated NRF2 in squalene-mediated cytoprotection. However, the molecular basis through which squalene may engage the NRF2 regulatory pathway remains incompletely understood. Here, we investigated the structural feasibility of a potential interaction between squalene and the KEAP1 Kelch domain using molecular docking across three human KEAP1 crystal structures (PDB IDs: 6TYM, 6SP4 and 5CGJ). The docking protocol was evaluated through native-ligand redocking, yielding RMSD values of 0.826, 0.277 and 0.303 A, respectively. Squalene was consistently accommodated within the canonical hydrophobic cavity, with predicted docking scores of 7.905, 7.513 and 6.756 kcal/mol. The predicted interaction environment was predominantly hydrophobic and involved residues including Arg415, Arg380 and Asn414, without conventional hydrogen-bond formation. These findings support the structural feasibility of squalene accommodation within the KEAP1 Kelch domain and provide a testable hypothesis connecting stress-responsive squalene metabolism with potential KEAP1 NRF2 regulation. However, docking alone does not establish direct binding, physiological accessibility, KEAP1 inhibition or functional NRF2 activation. Further biophysical, molecular-dynamics and cellular investigations are required to establish the biological significance of the predicted interaction.

papers.title: Optimization of a Subcutaneous Epithelioid Hemangioendothelioma Xenograft Model for Evaluation of Preclinical Therapeutics
papers.abstract: Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma (EHE) is an ultra-rare vascular sarcoma characterized by an unpredictable clinical trajectory and lack of established standard-of-care treatment regimens. Despite the pressing need for effective therapeutic strategies, the scarcity of clinically relevant preclinical models remains a major barrier to drug development. To address this challenge, we used a patient-derived human EHE cell line to optimize and validate a subcutaneous xenograft model in mice. Optimization of cell-inoculation density revealed that injection of high cell densities was associated with adverse systemic responses and primary tumour growth kinetics unsuitable for longitudinal drug screening. In contrast, inoculation of low, sub-million cell densities generated reproducible xenografts that followed classical sigmoidal growth kinetics, providing a suitable therapeutic window for comparative treatment studies. Subsequent histopathological analysis confirmed that the tumours were highly proliferative and retained key features of EHE pathology, including expression of the EHE-associated markers ERG and CAMTA1. Treatment response validation further demonstrated sensitivity to mTOR inhibition, a characteristic preserved from the original patient-derived sample. Treatment with nab-sirolimus significantly suppressed tumour growth and reduced phosphorylation of ribosomal protein S6, consistent with suppression of downstream mTORC1 signalling. In this study, the optimized CDX model retains key EHE features and provides an extended observation window with sustained growth of untreated controls, supporting longitudinal assessment of antitumour activity and pharmacodynamic responses. This platform provides a practical framework for evaluating and comparing candidate therapies for EHE.

papers.title: Early Progression Cells mark a stem-like state associated with pancreatic cancer initiation and progression
papers.abstract: Pancreatic cancer is deemed to progress from microscopic pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PanINs). However, low grade PanINs are frequently detected in the general population without presentation or increased risk of developing cancer, suggesting that many PanINs never progress to tumours. What precisely characterises PanINs that develop into tumours is insufficiently understood. Using a mouse model where pancreatitis-induced tissue injury promotes pancreatic cancer from rare KrasG12D cells, we identify Early Progression Cells (EPCs) as a new entity, a novel population of cancer stem-like cells. Transcriptomic analyses illustrate EPCs as stress-adapted, inflammation responsive stem cells that also upregulate gene programmes indicative of microenvironment remodelling. Using identified EPC protein markers, we show that EPCs are prevalent in early metaplastic stages and in PanIN progression from low grade to high grade but are rarer in tumours. PanIN- and tumour-derived sphere and organoid assays demonstrate that EPCs possess all characteristics of stem cells in vitro and are dependent on Nupr1 stress response pathways for survival and growth. We identify APP-CD74 as a novel cell-cell interaction pathway between EPCs and neighbouring epithelial cells in PanINs and tumours. Inhibition of CD74 activity in vitro induces high-grade PanIN organoid death, suggesting EPCs are critical for high-grade PanINs. Using spatial transcriptomics of human samples, we detect gene signatures of EPCs in distinct regions of human PanIN and PDAC tissues, including APP-CD74 interactions, providing compelling evidence that EPCs are relevant to human disease. Further understanding of EPC biology will likely uncover new knowledge on why rare PanINs progress towards tumours.

papers.title: ALIGN: A modular framework for quantitative analysis of longitudinal development in Caenorhabditis elegans
papers.abstract: Longitudinal live imaging is a powerful tool for studying growth, development and behaviour. However, reproducible and scalable analysis of the large resulting datasets remains a major bottleneck. Here, we present ALIGN (Automated Longitudinal Image-based Growth aNalyzer), a modular framework that integrates deep learning-based segmentation, automated quality control, computational straightening, feature extraction and interactive annotation within a single configurable pipeline that can be operated end-to-end by users without coding expertise. Applying ALIGN to longitudinal development of C. elegans, we demonstrate accurate segmentation across heterogeneous imaging conditions, detection of larval stage transitions from growth trajectories, and data-driven quality control, ensuring high measurement precision. Computational straightening and alignment enable consistent analysis of motile animals, removing motion artefacts from three-dimensional optical sectioning. Applying ALIGN to measure pharyngeal pumping and growth rates in wild-type and eat-2 mutants uncovered a non-proportional relationship between feeding and growth. ALIGN thus provides generalizable tools and resources for longitudinal, single-animal analysis of development.

papers.title: HOX13 factors shape cell developmental transcriptional program through multiple mechanisms that regulate chromatin accessibility.
papers.abstract: HOX transcription factors pattern embryonic tissues and organs and have post-developmental roles in adult tissue maintenance and function. They can bind inaccessible chromatin, but their roles in chromatin accessibility remain unclear. Using in vivo and in vitro approaches, we show that HOX13 factors promote both initial opening and maintenance of accessibility at subsets of target regulatory elements. Mechanistically, the HOX13-dependent chromatin accessibility involves both its homodimerization and the recruitment of the SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complex. Our findings indicate that SWI/SNF contributes to the extent of opening but is neither sufficient nor the sole determinant of HOXA13 pioneering activity. In iPSCs, HOXA13 induction rapidly reduces pluripotency gene expression while activating an early osteochondrogenic transcriptional program, which, at least in part, corresponds to direct gene regulation by HOXA13. Together, these findings identify multiple, context-dependent contributions to HOX13-mediated chromatin regulation, resulting in early lineage-associated responses.

papers.title: Podoplanin shapes epidermal morphogenesis and coordinates stem cell and epidermal-dermal responses during inflammatory remodelling
papers.abstract: Skin development and adaptation to inflammatory stress require keratinocytes to coordinate changes in cell behaviour with tissue organisation. Cell adhesion and the cortical cytoskeleton support the structural plasticity underlying these responses. Here, using complementary mouse models of global podoplanin deletion and conditional deletion in basal keratinocytes driven by keratin 5-Cre (K5Cre), we identify a role for the small transmembrane glycoprotein podoplanin in maintaining basal layer organisation and coordinating differentiation with barrier acquisition during development, as well as in inflammatory skin remodelling. Podoplanin expression was dynamically regulated during epidermal morphogenesis, becoming enriched in basal epithelial compartments before declining postnatally in the interfollicular epidermis. Both deletion models exhibited basal layer disorganisation, altered division orientation and increased epidermal thickness. Premature or expanded expression of differentiation markers was accompanied by delayed barrier acquisition, indicating that podoplanin loss uncouples differentiation marker expression from functional maturation. Barrier function subsequently recovered despite persistent histological abnormalities. In primary keratinocytes, podoplanin deficiency disrupted junctional actin organisation, reduced ERM phosphorylation and impaired junctional enrichment of pERM and doubly phosphorylated myosin light chain 2 (ppMLC2), despite largely preserved recruitment of adhesion proteins. In adult skin, K5Cre-mediated deletion altered differentiation marker dynamics following topical application of the proinflammatory agent 12-O-tetradecanoylphorbol-13-acetate (TPA), while the epidermal thickening response remained largely comparable to controls. These epidermal changes were accompanied by altered dermal thickness dynamics and an absence of TPA-induced podoplanin expression in dermal fibroblasts. Furthermore, TPA reduced the number of BrdU-retaining cells in the interfollicular epidermis of controls but not K5Cre-mediated conditional podoplanin knockout mice. This difference is consistent with impaired activation or mobilisation of slow-cycling cells, suggesting altered responsiveness within the epidermal stem and progenitor compartment. Together, these findings establish keratinocyte-expressed podoplanin as a regulator of epidermal organisation and functional maturation, with effects extending beyond the epithelium to shape the dermal response to inflammatory challenge.

papers.title: Genetic disruption of cutaneous de novo glucocorticoid synthesis: a CRISPR-Cas9 CYP11B1-knockout human epidermal model
papers.abstract: Human skin functions as both a physical barrier and a neuroendocrine and steroidogenic organ. Glucocorticoids (GC) synthesized in the skin help to maintain skin immune homeostasis and to mediate responses to environmental stressors. Cutaneous GC synthesis has so far been disrupted only pharmacologically, with inhibitors that do not discriminate CYP11B1 from its close paralogue CYP11B2, or genetically in mouse keratinocytes, so the consequences of blocking this pathway in human keratinocytes remain untested. Here, we disrupted de novo GC synthesis by knocking out the CYP11B1 gene using CRISPR-Cas9, thereby interrupting the terminal enzymatic process of converting 11-deoxycortisol to cortisol in mitochondria. Two independent knockout clones were established, one carrying a 28 bp deletion spanning the start codon and one carrying a multi-exon deletion. Both clones reconstituted stratified 3D epidermal models as in wild-type models, indicating that loss of CYP11B1 does not by itself impair epidermal differentiation. Wild-type models responded with increased CYP11B1 transcript abundance and immunofluorescence signal, whereas both knockout clones retained a UVB-inducible transcript signal but showed no detectable CYP11B1 protein, confirming loss of the protein product at the tissue level. This work provides, to our knowledge, the first human keratinocyte model carrying a genomically defined block in de novo GC synthesis, and a tissue-level platform for resolving the role of keratinocyte-derived GC in epidermal homeostasis and environmental stress responses.

papers.title: Systematic comparison of genetically encoded F-actin probes for visualizing actomyosin dynamics in vivo using C. elegans
papers.abstract: Genetically encoded F-actin probes enable visualization of actin organization and dynamics in living cells, but their performance and effects on cellular function can vary by probe, fluorescent protein, and biological context. Here, we systematically compared three F-actin probes - F-tractin, LifeAct, and Utrophin - fused to mScarlet-I, mNeonGreen, or mStayGold in vivo, using Caenorhabditis elegans. We used single-copy transgenic strains and evaluated fluorescence intensity, photostability, developmental and reproductive outcomes, cytokinetic ring closure, and probe localization across diverse cellular contexts. mStayGold provided the greatest brightness and photostability, making it well suited for long-term time-lapse imaging, whereas mNeonGreen offers an alternative for applications requiring photobleaching. Most of the strains exhibited minimal detectable effects on development and cellular function and outperformed previously generated strains tested. Probe performance varied across tissues and developmental stages. F-tractin generally exhibited lower fluorescence intensity than LifeAct and Utrophin, particularly in embryos. Although the probes largely exhibited subcellular localization patterns consistent with phalloidin staining, differences in their labeling of specific F-actin structures were observed. Together, these results establish a practical framework for selecting genetically encoded F-actin probes for C. elegans, they suggest best candidates for other in vivo systems, and they highlight the importance of considering both fluorescent protein and actin-binding probe when designing live-cell imaging experiments.

papers.title: The FDA-approved CDK4/6 inhibitor Abemaciclib is a potent agonist of the β-arrestin-biased atypical chemokine receptor ACKR3
papers.abstract: Atypical chemokine receptor 3 (ACKR3/CXCR7) is an intrinsically {beta}-arrestin-biased family-A GPCR that controls chemokine availability by scavenging CXCL12 and CXCL11, and consequently plays a key role in cancer, chronic inflammation, autoimmunity, cardiovascular disease, and CNS repair. Despite its pathophysiological significance, the chemical space available to interrogate and therapeutically modulate this receptor remains limited. Here, by using a drug-repurposing strategy to screen 2,342 FDA-approved compounds in a NanoBRET-based fluorescent chemokine-binding competition assay, we identified the clinically used CDK4/6 inhibitor abemaciclib (Verzenios(R)) as a nanomolar ACKR3 ligand. Abemaciclib inhibited CXCL12 binding to ACKR3 with comparable affinity to the ACKR3-reference agonist VUF15485, whereas the related clinically used CDK4/6 inhibitors palbociclib, ribociclib, dalpiciclib and trilaciclib were inactive on this receptor. Binding and functional profiling across classical and atypical chemokine receptors revealed selectivity for ACKR3, including lack of detectable activity at the CXCL12 receptors CXCR4 and ACKR5. Abemaciclib acted as a potent ACKR3 agonist, recruiting both {beta}-arrestin-1 and 2 and promoting rapid receptor internalization with potencies and efficacies, like the reference ACKR3 agonist VUF15485. Major CYP3A4-derived abemaciclib metabolites retained ACKR3 binding and agonist activity, albeit with reduced potency. Methionine 13C-HSQC NMR confirmed direct receptor engagement and revealed a small-molecule-like ACKR3 conformational signature distinct from the CXCL12-bound state. Cryo-EM of the abemaciclib-ACKR3-CID24 complex at 3.2 [A] uncovered a unique, inverted U-shaped ligand binding pose in the orthosteric pocket and activation-associated rearrangements of TM6, TM7 and helix 8. Functionally, abemaciclib blocked ACKR3-mediated uptake of CXCL11 and CXCL12 in vitro. Moreover, oral administration of abemaciclib in mice resulted in a time-dependent increase in plasma CXCL12 levels, indicative of in vivo ACKR3 target engagement. These findings establish this FDA-approved kinase inhibitor as a potent ACKR3 modulator and reveal an unexpected pharmacological link of this CDK4/6 inhibitor to atypical chemokine receptor biology.

papers.title: CryoID2: deep learning-enhanced identification of protein and RNA from cryoEM maps
papers.abstract: Identifying the molecular components of cryoEM/cryoET maps of endogenous or poorly characterized complexes remains a major bottleneck. CryoID2 addresses this by integrating deep learning-based feature prediction with sequence prioritization and structural evaluation. Three 3D U-Nets extract structure classes, key-atom positions, and reduced residue/nucleotide types from the input map. These predictions support backbone tracing and the generation of short sequence queries that rank candidates from a user-supplied pool-using BLASTp for proteins and a maximin strategy for RNA. Corresponding PDB or AlphaFold models are then retrieved, rigidly fitted using predicted features and experimental density, and ranked by map agreement. Module-level tests show high-recall feature prediction and resolution-dependent atom clustering, while a 52-case benchmark recovers near-reference fitting quality. In practice, cryoID2 correctly identified PfA-M17 from a 166-protein mass-spectrometry pool and the unannotated Ca-raiA RNA from a genome-derived non-coding sequence set, demonstrating a unified sequence-plus-structure route to molecular identification in cryoEM maps.

papers.title: Tn-Seq-based identification of genes that play a role in antimicrobial tolerance of Pseudomonas aeruginosa aggregates
papers.abstract: Microbial biofilms, whether surface-associated or in the form of aggregated microbes, cause a variety of persistent infections due to their inherent tolerance to antibiotic treatment. Current knowledge of the mechanistic basis of biofilm-associated antibiotic tolerance is fragmented, and the relative importance of previously identified factors remains unknown. We developed a Tn-Seq-based workflow that enables simultaneous assessment of the relative antibiotic tolerance of thousands of individual clonal bacterial aggregates, each established by a single transposon mutant. Using this genome-wide Tn-Seq analysis approach, we identified several factors and pathways that play a role in antimicrobial tolerance of Pseudomonas aeruginosa aggregates. The majority of these factors are important for aggregate-associated tolerance to specific antibiotics, whereas some factors play a role in aggregate-associated tolerance regardless of the class of antibiotic. This methodology provides a framework that can be adapted to investigate aggregate-associated tolerance for other bacterial species and in response to different antimicrobial agents and stressors.

papers.title: Role of Very Long-Chain Fatty Acyl-Ceramides in Endocytic Uptake
papers.abstract: Specialized endoplasmic reticulum (ER) subdomains termed ER sterol exit sites (ERSES), transiently contact endocytic sites to locally supply sterols, which in turn initiate actin polymerization and drive membrane invagination. Osh2, an oxysterol-binding protein (OSBP)-related protein (ORP), mediates the non-vesicular sterol transfer at ER-endocytic contact sites (ER-ECS). In search for additional ERSES components, we identified Fat1, a fatty acid (FA) transporter and acyl-CoA synthetase with specificity for very long-chain (VLC) FAs (C20-C26). Analysis of VLC-FA anabolic and catabolic pathways revealed a specific requirement for VLC fatty acyl-ceramides (VLCA-Cers) in the constriction of endocytic invaginations. Strikingly, the Cer synthase physically interacted with the endocytic machinery, pointing to a direct role of VLCFA-Cers in membrane remodelling. Consistent with this view, molecular dynamics and live-cell imaging of a Cer probe indicated that the ORPs Osh1 and Osh3 contribute to Cer export from at ER-ECS and and that their depletion recapitulates the endocytic defects observed in the absence of VLCFA-Cer. Our findings establish that local transport of VLCA-Cers is required for endocytic budding and reveal ERSES as hubs where Cer and sterol biosynthesis and transport converge

papers.title: Particle-Associated Prokaryotic Community Structures in the Bering and Chukchi Seas
papers.abstract: Free-living and particle-associated bacteria play distinct roles in the cycling of organic matter, but how these lifestyles are partitioned in the highly productive, rapidly warming Bering and Chukchi Seas is largely unknown. During the Arctic Shelf Growth, Advection, Respiration and Deposition Rate Experiments (ASGARD) cruise in June 2017, a period of anomalously warm sea surface temperatures, we collected 78 samples at three depths (surface, middle, and bottom) at 12 process stations and sequentially filtered them onto 20 {micro}m, 3 {micro}m, and 0.2 {micro}m filters. Using 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing and hierarchical clustering of amplicon sequence variant (ASV) relative abundances, we resolved four sample clusters. Although pore size was not used to build the clusters, communities separated into a free-living cluster associated mainly with Anadyr Water (FL1; 0.2 {micro}m fraction) and three particle-associated clusters (PA1-PA3; 3 and 20 {micro}m fractions), several of which were enriched in Bacteroidia. Alphaproteobacteria, Gammaproteobacteria, and Bacteroidia were present in all size fractions, with Gammaproteobacteria most biased toward the free-living fraction. Community structure did not differ with depth, consistent with the shallow, weakly stratified shelf, and distance-based redundancy analysis identified salinity as the sole significant environmental factor distinguishing communities. These results suggest that lifestyle and water-mass origin, rather than depth, structure size-fractionated bacterial communities on the Pacific Arctic shelf, and that freshening and changes in bloom dynamics could reshape particle-associated communities in this region.

papers.title: Factors affecting microbial community composition in Split Lake, MB, Canada
papers.abstract: Split Lake is a large freshwater lake in northern Manitoba, Canada, that receives major inflows from the Nelson River, Burntwood River, and Grassy River. In 1976, during the Churchill River Diversion (CRD) project, most of the water in the Churchill River was diverted into the Nelson River via the Rat River, and the Burntwood River, creating a large inflow pressure in the lower Nelson area, including Split Lake. Decades after its implementation, the Churchill River Diversion still influences ecological and environmental processes in the area. In this study, metabarcoding of the 16S rRNA gene was employed to characterize the microbial community structure of the lake. Environmental factors (temperature, pH, turbidity, dissolved oxygen) and cyanotoxin levels were also assessed. The objectives of this study were to establish a baseline for microbiota across the lake and examine how environmental variables affect microbial population dynamics. The study was conducted in the summer of 2024, encompassing 14 sites on Split Lake and 2 sites on Assean Lake, an adjacent waterbody with minimal influence from hydroelectric infrastructure. Split Lake was found to harbor six distinct microbial clusters, with turbidity and dissolved oxygen levels correlating with different aquatic regimes within the lake. The predominant taxa in Split Lake included Actinobacteria hgcI clade and Cyanobium. Microcystin concentrations measured throughout the study were always below the Maximum Acceptable Concentration (MAC) set for Canadian federal drinking water standards.

papers.title: COSMOS: integrated vector-pathogen metagenomics for mosquito-borne disease
papers.abstract: By 2050, almost half of the global population will be at risk of mosquito-borne disease. Effective response requires monitoring both pathogen transmission and vector abundance, yet these are typically assessed using separate assays with limited taxonomic breadth. Here we present COSMOS (COmprehensive Sequencing for MOSquito-borne disease), a targeted metagenomics workflow designed to reconstruct pathogen genomes and mosquito community composition directly from mixed field-collected samples. Over three annual rounds of a major Australian surveillance program, we evaluated >120,000 mosquitoes in 219 traps, with 98.7% agreement with surveillance data across seven monitored arboviruses, and additional detections of Sindbis virus and the state's first detection of encephalitic Little Sussex virus. Of 137 viral detections, 101 yielded near-complete genomes (>90% coverage) at median 95x depth. Using an accompanying computational workflow, COSMOS quantified mosquito composition, matching entomological estimates of reported vector species (CCC 0.78-0.89). Joint analysis of virus and vector composition identified structured mosquito communities associated with spatial and temporal environmental variation, allowing the ecological context of arbovirus detections to be characterised. Detections during the Murray Valley encephalitis virus outbreak in 2023 were concentrated within a narrowly defined mosquito-community space corresponding to rural communities dominated by the inland S-AUS sub-lineage of Culex annulirostris. Integrated vector-pathogen metagenomics provides ecological and evolutionary context for arbovirus activity within a single scalable workflow for surveillance and outbreak response.

papers.title: Intrinsic timekeeping in Escherichia coli
papers.abstract: Circadian clocks allow organisms to anticipate predictable environmental changes across the day-night cycle. Here we show that the bacterium Escherichia coli exhibits intrinsic timekeeping that anticipates daily temperature cycles. E. coli biofilms entrained to daily temperature shifts, producing 24-hour rhythms in curli plaque formation that persisted under constant temperature. Mechanistically, genetic analyses localized the autonomous timing machinery to the Rcs phosphorelay, which exhibits structural and conceptual parallels with other circadian systems. The BluFR sensory pathway, which acts upstream of the Rcs phosphorelay, linked temperature and blue-light cycles to rhythmic curli production. Flagellar promoter activity and curli production peaked at opposite times of day, suggesting daily coordination of adhesion and motility programs. These findings identify an intrinsic timing system in E. coli that expands our understanding of biological timekeeping.

papers.title: KDM6A is enzymatically active at the Golgi apparatus where it is necessary for maintenance of Golgi apparatus morphology
papers.abstract: KDM6A and KDM6B, lysine demethylases, play a central role in regulation of transcription through their demethylation activity towards H3K27me3 and have also been shown to be dynamically regulated upon epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT). In particular, KDM6A has been implicated in a variety of malignancies and is frequently mutated in cancers including those in kidney, bladder, colorectal, and breast. KDM6A and KDM6B function as part of the COMPASS-like protein complex (CLC) which includes methyltransferases KMT2C/KMT2D and the regulatory WRAD-subcomplex. KDM6A total protein is known to be suppressed by TGF-{beta} in MCF10A breast cells; however, our examination of protein localization by immunofluorescence and LC-MS/MS reveals that KDM6A expression is lost in the nucleus but retained in the Golgi apparatus, independent of other CLC complex members. Importantly, KDM6A isolated from a biochemically-separated subcellular membranous fraction possesses the catalytic JmjC domain and is enzymatically active, indicating that KDM6A may have non-nuclear substrates. Further, knockdown of KDM6A and treatment with TGF-{beta} similarly alter Golgi apparatus morphology, in a cell type specific manner, suggesting context-dependent regulatory functions. These findings support a model in which KDM6A is necessary to maintain Golgi apparatus morphology and is enzymatically active outside of the nucleus.

papers.title: PHYRE, a Translated uORF, is Required for Phytochrome B Translation and Photomorphogenesis in Arabidopsis
papers.abstract: Translational control allows cells to adjust protein output independently of transcription, yet the mRNA-encoded mechanisms that govern this regulatory layer remain poorly understood. Upstream open reading frames (uORFs) are among the most prevalent translational regulatory elements in eukaryotic genomes; however, characterised examples of activating uORFs that promote rather than inhibit downstream translation are exceedingly rare. Here we show that efficient expression of phytochrome B (phyB), the master red-light photoreceptor of Arabidopsis thaliana, requires translation of a short uORF in its own 5'UTR, which we name PHYTOCHROME REGULATOR (PHYRE). Loss of PHYRE function phenocopies phyB null mutants across germination, hypocotyl growth, leaf development, and flowering time. PHYRE activity depends on its encoded peptide sequence, and the spacing between PHYRE and the PHYB start codon is a critical determinant of downstream translation efficiency, consistent with a position-dependent reinitiation mechanism. PHYRE-like elements are conserved across eudicots, establishing uORF-mediated translational gating as a broadly maintained regulatory layer controlling a master photoreceptor.

papers.title: MET inhibition exploits conserved regulatory dependencies in malignant rhabdoid tumors
papers.abstract: Malignant rhabdoid tumors (MRTs) are lethal, yet genomically simple childhood cancers characterised by universal SWI/SNF dysregulation. Despite this shared molecular framework, the regulatory programs sustaining MRTs and how they wire actionable dependencies, remain poorly defined. Here, we integrated single-cell multi-omic profiling and spatial transcriptomics across anatomically and molecularly diverse MRTs, generating a comprehensive multimodal MRT dataset at single-cell resolution. We leveraged this resource to identify candidate tumor-specific dependencies, which were subsequently functionally validated in vitro and in vivo in matched patient-derived models. We found that distinct malignant subpopulations are spatially patterned in complex environmentally shaped topologies, consistent with reciprocal interactions with stromal and immune compartments contributing to intratumoral transcriptional diversity. We identified recurrent transcriptional metaprograms conserved across patients and molecular subtypes, including a previously undescribed shared core rhabdoid program, as well as a metaprogram characterized by extracellular matrix interactions, and preferentially localized in tumor-stroma intermixed neighborhoods, supporting identification of niche conditioning cues. Mechanistically, we identified regulatory wiring driving these metaprograms, with the core shared rhabdoid programme coordinated by a circuit centred on TCF12, ZNF148 and CHD2. Guided by target nominations from our integrated analyses, we performed a curated drug screen using patient-derived MRT models and validated HGF/MET signaling as a selective vulnerability in extrarenal rhabdoid tumors. Pharmacologic MET inhibition was cytotoxic in sensitive models and induced a complete response in vivo using a clinically approved compound. Importantly, MET expression in primary tumors correlated with response, supporting biomarker-guided patient stratification for immediate clinical translation. Collectively, our findings define the molecular architecture of MRTs, reveal conserved regulatory programs beyond anatomical and molecular subtypes, and highlight a targetable signaling axis with immediate translational potential, establishing a framework for precision therapy in this lethal pediatric malignancy.

papers.title: Glioblastoma model mouse rescue from mortality by brain-targeted catalytically-enhanced angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 mutant-antibody fusion protein
papers.abstract: We have discovered that an engineered angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2)-brain-targeted antibody fusion protein, referred to as ACE2dm-s1, improves survival of CT-2A xenograft glioblastoma (GBM) model mice when administered in combination with a small molecule STING agonist cancer therapeutic. Particularly striking about these survival results is that prior efforts that used losartan, a small molecule angiotensin receptor antagonist that acts on the same Renin-Angiotensin System (RAS) axis that is affected by the action of ACE2dm-s1, showed that this small molecule provided no survival benefit when used as an element of combination therapy in the same CT-2A GBM model used in our experiments. The improved CT-2A mouse survival, which was not observed for ACE2dm-s1 or STING agonist monotherapy, combines with our flow cytometry study results that revealed an ACE2dm-s1-mediated shift of brain immune cell populations toward an anti-tumoral composition to establish ACE2dm-s1's utility as a tumor microenvironment (TME) modulator that could serve as an adjuvant in increasing the efficacy of wide range of cancer treatment modalities including chemotherapeutic agents, immune checkpoint inhibitors, and CAR-T cells.

papers.title: The Pregnane X Receptor (PXR) contributes to phenotypic plasticity and modulates the sensitivity to targeted therapies in melanoma
papers.abstract: The challenge in treating advanced metastatic melanoma lies in the development of therapeutic resistance and the risk of recurrence. Understanding the mechanisms underlying tumor adaptation to treatment is therefore crucial, as they can directly influence therapeutic efficacy. Tolerance to targeted therapies may be influenced by drug transport and metabolism within tumors, processes regulated by numerous genes under the transcriptional control of the nuclear receptor PXR (Pregnane X Receptor, NR1I2). We revealed, for the first time, significant and heterogeneous expression of PXR in human melanoma samples. We previously showed that PXR can be activated by BRAF inhibitors (BRAFi), but not by MEK inhibitors (MEKi), which are currently used in combination for the treatment of BRAF-V600E-mutated melanoma. Here, we investigated whether PXR expression influences melanoma cell sensitivity to MAPK pathway inhibitors. Using BRAF-mutated human melanoma cell lines, we showed that stable PXR expression sensitizes cells to combined BRAFi/MEKi treatment. Transcriptomic analysis further revealed that PXR expression is associated with the upregulation of several phenotypic markers, with MITF identified as a major regulator in untreated PXR-overexpressing cells. These findings suggest that PXR promotes a shift toward a melanocytic phenotype, which is associated with increased sensitivity to BRAFi/MEKi treatment. Characterization of the PXR-associated transcriptional signature in melanoma may therefore have translational value for identifying patients more likely to benefit from targeted therapies and support the development of PXR as a predictive biomarker of therapeutic response.

papers.title: Adaptation and conservation of turtle visual opsins over a deep phylogenetic divergence
papers.abstract: The ecological radiation of organisms in diverse light environments depends, in part, on adaptive alterations within visual systems, particularly retinal photoreceptors and their visual pigments. Evidence of visual adaptation occurs across vertebrate lineages but is notably lacking in turtles, despite their complex visual system with up to eight photoreceptor cell types and five visual pigments. This lack of knowledge is especially pronounced in side-neck turtles (Pleurodira), as nearly all information on turtle vision derives from hidden-neck turtles (Cryptodira). Here, we bridge this ~200-million-year evolutionary gap by investigating visual opsin evolution using an eye transcriptome and whole-genome sequences from 59 turtle species spanning both suborders, as well as an additional 42 representative reptile species. We estimated selective pressures using codon-based evolutionary models, testing for positive selection and long-term shifts between turtles and other reptiles, between suborders, and among major habitat types. We also analysed spectral tuning sites to assess how spectral sensitivity diverged between and within suborders. Our analyses revealed remarkably conserved turtle visual opsin sequences, with phylogeny-wide positive selection detected only in LWS. Habitat explained more shifts in selective pressure than taxonomy, with long-term shifts detected across all five opsins. Spectral tuning sites predict conserved UV sensitivity of SWS1 across cryptodirans, consistent with the few species previously characterised, whereas shared changes identified in pleurodirans predict violet sensitivity, revealing previously unrecognized divergence in short-wavelength vision between turtle suborders. This study advances our understanding of turtle visual system evolution and highlights the need for conservation strategies that account for their distinct visual capabilities.

papers.title: Oocyte-stored Mif promotes preimplantation development as an embryonic extracellular signal
papers.abstract: Mammalian preimplantation embryos develop more efficiently in groups than in isolation, suggesting that embryos secrete embryotrophic factors that promote development. However, the endogenous embryotrophic signals responsible for this long-recognized phenomenon remain incompletely defined. Using an unbiased proteomic screen for stable maternal proteins that may function as embryonic extracellular signals, we identified the cytokine macrophage migration inhibitory factor (Mif) as an abundant oocyte-stored protein that persists for several days after fertilization in mice. Quantitative measurements of spent culture medium reveal that developing embryos release Mif, with a substantial fraction derived from the maternal deposit. Extracellular Mif levels peak 3-4 days post fertilization, the same period when Mif knockout preimplantation embryos produce its strongest phenotype. Embryos lacking maternal, but not zygotic, Mif display defective blastocyst growth even in group culture. Individually cultured embryos exhibit similar blastocyst growth defects that can be rescued by supplementing recombinant Mif at physiologically relevant concentrations. Mif activates the PI3K-Akt-mTORC1 pathway through the cell-surface receptor Cd74 to promote blastocyst growth and cell proliferation. Together, these findings identify Mif as a potential endogenous contributor to the density-dependent embryotrophic effects and reveal that maternally stored proteins may function long after fertilization as extracellular signaling molecules to support preimplantation development in mammals.

papers.title: Physiological caffeine concentrations do not affect enteric neural crest cell migration in a mouse model
papers.abstract: The defect in enteric neural crest cell (ENCCs) migration that causes Hirschsprung disease (HD) in newborns is linked to genetic and likely also environmental factors. Among these, maternal coffee consumption has been associated with increased HD risk, yet the role of caffeine on ENCC migration has remained unexplored. Here, we show that although mouse ENCCs express caffeine-sensitive ADORA2A receptors, physiological doses of caffeine do not perturb endogenous ENCC calcium activity. We find that caffeine can modulate ENCC outgrowth in a 2D culture model but that it does not affect migration in a 3D collagen gel and in the ex-vivo embryonic gut. We conclude that physiological doses of caffeine do not hamper ENCC migration in the ex-vivo embryonic mouse intestine, thereby discarding a potential direct environmental mechanism of caffeine in HD.

papers.title: Single-cell transcriptomics of enriched rare neural lineages of Tribolium castaneum
papers.abstract: Background Single-cell transcriptomic atlases have transformed our understanding of cell diversity. However, studies designed to profile entire tissues or organisms often omit or underrepresent rare cell populations. Enriching selected populations before sequencing offers a powerful approach to overcoming this limitation, but its application in insects has largely focused on Drosophila, limiting opportunities for comparative studies. Here, we establish complementary workflows for targeted transcriptomic profiling of rare neural populations in the red flour beetle, Tribolium castaneum. Results We developed two workflows combining population enrichment with single-cell or single-nucleus RNA sequencing. First, we generated cell suspensions from a transgenic reporter line labelling embryonic neuroblasts, enriched fluorescently labelled cells by fluorescence-activated cell sorting, and performed single-cell RNA sequencing. Second, we immunolabelled first-instar larval brains with an antibody against the nuclear transcription factor Rx, isolated and sorted labelled nuclei, and performed single-nucleus RNA sequencing. Both workflows yielded material suitable for transcriptomic profiling, demonstrating complementary reporter-based and antibody-based strategies for accessing selected neural populations at different developmental stages. Conclusions These workflows establish a methodological framework for targeted single-cell and single-nucleus transcriptomic studies of rare or specific neural populations in Tribolium. They provide practical starting points for adaptation to other insect systems, expanding opportunities for comparative investigations of neural development and cell-type evolution.

papers.title: In vivo effects of inducible transgene expression of the age-associated glycogenes St6gal1 and Man1a on epidermal homeostasis
papers.abstract: Glycosylation of cell-surface proteins plays several essential roles in cell-matrix interactions and receptor signaling, thereby contributing to tissue homeostasis and aging. In aged mouse skin, epidermal stem cells exhibit increased levels of a2,6-sialylated complex-type N-glycans alongside upregulation of glycogenes such as St6gal1 and Man1a; however, the functional importance of these glycosylation changes in vivo remains largely unknown. Here, we generated doxycycline-inducible transgenic mice expressing the age-related glycogenes St6gal1 and Man1a, either individually or in combination, using ubiquitous and epidermis-specific drivers. Lectin-based analyses with SNA and rHeltuba demonstrated corresponding alterations in glycosylation patterns in these mice. Transgenic Man1a induction reduced epidermal proliferation and epidermal thickness. In contrast, St6gal1 induction caused splenomegaly and elevated expression of inflammatory signature genes in the skin but did not measurably alter epidermal proliferation or morphology. Double transgenic mice exhibited a hybrid phenotype combining inflammatory and proliferative impairments, although comparison of ubiquitous and epidermis-specific induction indicated that the observed skin phenotypes depended on the epidermal expression of the transgenes. An SNA lectin-based pull-down assay followed by mass spectrometry identified candidate a2,6-sialylated proteins, including integrin family members, junctional proteins, and surface receptors, following induction of St6gal1 and Man1a. Together, these findings suggest that increased expression of the age-associated glycogenes St6gal1 and Man1a perturbs distinct aspects of epidermal homeostasis in vivo and identify candidate glycoproteins that may mediate these effects.
